notes:
These are notes on Psalm 3, verse by verse. Two things to know first:

- **Gaps.** I found nothing on this psalm from Lutheran, Pentecostal, Anglican or Orthodox teachers. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, and no NET Bible or Bible Odyssey notes. Those sections are left out.
- **Labels.** Where I call a writer "Methodist," the page itself doesn't say so unless I note that it does. Treat those labels as my own.

---

**Title (superscription)**

- Guzik says this is the first psalm in the book with a title. Following Boice, he says the titles are part of the Hebrew text and should be taken seriously. The story behind it is in 2 Samuel 15–18. This is the first psalm with a title: A Psalm of David when he fled from Absalom his son. James Montgomery Boice points out that since these titles are in the canonical text of the Hebrew Bible, "They are to be taken with absolute seriousness throughout." The events are recorded in 2 Samuel 15-18 — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Precept Austin says this is the first of thirteen psalms whose titles name an event in David's life. It is also the first lament psalm and the first place "Selah" appears.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-3-commentary
- Bible.org notes that some scholars call Psalm 3 a morning psalm and Psalm 4 an evening psalm. It suggests David may have written it just after crossing the Jordan.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-3-when-life-falls-apart
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Augustine reads the whole psalm as spoken by Christ. He says verse 5 fits the Passion and Resurrection better than David's flight.  He takes Absalom's name to mean "a father's peace." He links Absalom to Judas, to whom Christ showed peace even as Judas betrayed him.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm

**v. 1**

- Spurgeon points to 2 Samuel 15:12: Absalom's following kept growing while David's troops kept shrinking.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Guzik notes that many of David's former friends deserted him and joined the rebels.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Bible.org: God already knew all this, but David still tells Him. He isn't informing God; he is handing his burden over and admitting he can't cope alone.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-3-when-life-falls-apart
- A Christ-centred reading: Spurgeon's notes apply the verse to the crowds who seized Jesus and shouted "Crucify him."  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Augustine sees the enemies' numbers growing even to include one of Christ's own disciples.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm

**v. 2**

- Guzik thinks the critics didn't doubt that God *could* help David. They thought God was *unwilling*, because of David's past sin. Shimei is an example (2 Samuel 16:7–8).  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Spurgeon calls this the most bitter of all afflictions: fearing there is no help for us in God. He adds that Christ felt this most deeply when He cried "My God, why hast thou forsaken me?"  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Matthew Henry reads the critics differently. He says they spoke as if David's danger were too great for God Himself to handle.  He also notes the Hebrew word behind "help" is really "salvation."  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_003.cfm
- One StudyLight note says Old Testament "deliverance" or "salvation" usually means rescue from a physical danger, not salvation to eternal life.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/3-2.html
- Augustine: if the enemies had thought He would rise again, they would never have killed Him.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
- **What "Selah" means is disputed:**
  - Guzik: most likely a pause to reflect; possibly a musical interlude.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
  - Spurgeon's notes: the meaning isn't settled. The Aramaic Targum renders it "for ever," and the Latin Vulgate leaves it out.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
  - Calvin (Reformed) links it to a root meaning "to lift up." He thinks it marks the voices rising together in song.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/3-2.html
  - Wesley (Methodist, per the Wesley Center page) says it usually stands at a striking point, perhaps to wake up the singer and hearer.  — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/

**v. 3**

- Guzik: this isn't a request. It is a bold statement of fact.  David's circumstances held nothing glorious or encouraging; his God did.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Precept Austin, quoting Krell: the shield was the Old Testament soldier's main defence, like a fortress he could carry.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-3-commentary
- Wesley reads the verse as looking forward. "My glory" means God has given, and will give again, reasons to boast in His power and favour. "Lifter up" means God will restore David's former power and dignity.  — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/
- Spurgeon's notes list ways God lifts the head: honour after shame, health after sickness, gladness after sorrow, restoration after a fall, victory after a setback.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Augustine's Latin reads "my taker." He takes it to mean the Word taking on human nature. He applies "lifter of my head" to Christ's human mind, which stayed united to the Word through the humiliation of the Passion.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm

**v. 4**

- **Praying out loud: a real difference.** Spurgeon says silent prayers are heard, but good people often pray better aloud, even in private.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
  Augustine says the "voice" here is the voice of the heart, not of the body. He cites Jesus' command to pray in secret.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
- **What is "His holy mountain"?**
  - Guzik: Absalom held Jerusalem, but he wasn't the one enthroned on God's hill. The Lord still held that ground.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
  - Wesley: heaven.  — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/
  - Henry: the ark of the covenant on Zion. He links it to Christ, set as King on that hill, through whom our prayers are heard.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_003.cfm
  - Augustine: most simply, God heard "out of His justice."  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
- Spurgeon's notes: in Scripture, for God to hear is the same as for Him to answer.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Maclaren: the verb tenses describe a habit and its steady result.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-3.html
- Precept Austin: the Selah after verse 4 contradicts the one after verse 2.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-3-commentary

**v. 5**

- **Traditional reading.** Guzik sees two blessings. Sleeping was one, given the pressure David was under. Waking was another, since many doubted he would live to see morning.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Henry: none of David's troubles cost him an hour's sleep, because the Lord upheld him.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_003.cfm
- Bible Hub: the Hebrew verb *samak*, "sustains," means supporting and upholding.  — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/3.htm
- **The Christ reading.** Augustine reads verse 5 as Christ freely giving Himself up to death and rising.  He also notes the verse mixes past and future tenses, which he takes as a sign of prophecy.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
- An older writer quoted in Spurgeon's notes (the page doesn't name him here) follows Augustine. He argues that "lying down" and "sleeping" here mean death, not ordinary sleep.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm

**v. 6**

- Guzik links the verse to Romans 8:31: "If God is for us, who can be against us?"  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Spurgeon's notes stress trusting God whatever things look like.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Augustine applies the verse to the crowds around Christ at the cross.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm

**v. 7**

- **"Arise."**
  - Cambridge Bible: these are the opening words of Israel's ancient marching cry from Numbers 10:35.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/3-7.htm
  - Guzik: a military phrase, calling God to defend Israel and lead it to victory.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
  - Augustine: God isn't asleep. Scripture describes Him by what He does in us.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm
  - Maclaren: David isn't so fearless that he no longer needs to pray.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-3.html
- **Past, present or future tense?** The BSB has a request ("Strike…"); older versions read "thou hast smitten."
  - Pulpit Commentary: God has always taken David's side in the past.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/3-7.htm
  - Ellicott prefers "thou smitest… breakest."  — https://biblehub.com/psalms/3-7.htm
  - Adam Clarke (I'm calling him Methodist; the page doesn't) reads "thou wilt smite": David is so sure of victory he speaks as if he already has it.  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/psalms/3-7.html
- **Insult, or making the enemy harmless?**
  - Barnes: the picture is of disarming a wild beast. It is not about insult.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/3-7.htm
  - Gill: a blow to the cheek shows contempt. He applies the verse to Christ's victory over sin, Satan, the world and death.  — same page
  - Keil and Delitzsch combine both ideas.  — same page
  - Ellicott compares the enemies to the lion and bear David fought as a boy.  — https://biblehub.com/psalms/3-7.htm
- Bible Hub: David isn't taking revenge himself. He leaves vengeance to the Lord.  — https://biblehub.com/psalms/3-7.htm
- Augustine reads the "teeth" as the curses spoken against the Son of God.  — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801003.htm

**v. 8**

- **Traditional reading.** Guzik: salvation, both final and immediate, belongs to God, not to any one nation or group.  David prayed for all God's people, not just himself.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-3/
- Bible.org: David wasn't relying on his troops, his advisers or his strategy.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-3-when-life-falls-apart
- **A real Protestant difference.**
  - Spurgeon (Baptist, Calvinist) calls this verse the heart of Calvinistic doctrine: salvation by grace alone.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
  - Adam Clarke says God's mercy saved His people, and it is His continued blessing that keeps them saved.  Clarke also says God's promises of salvation don't replace our prayers for it; they invite them.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/3-8.html
- Henry: God has declared His blessing on His people, and we should believe it rests on them even when we can't see its effects.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_003.cfm
- Spurgeon's notes point to the parallel in Jonah 2:9, "Salvation is of the Lord."  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps003.cfm
- Translations differ on the second line: some pray "may Your blessing be," others state "Your blessing is." The NET Bible has "you show favor to your people," and the Douay-Rheims (Catholic) has "thy blessing is upon thy people."  — https://biblehub.com/psalms/3-8.htm
